entries.evidence: The agent critic that ran this round is the installed plugin copy, version 6.14.65, whose tools line reads 'tools: Read, Grep' (<home>/.claude/plugins/cache/robotijn/ctoc/6.14.65/agents/pipeline/agent-critic.md, line 4). Every later round of every file meets the same limit until the installed plugin carries the approved grant. The human already chose to keep going with the installed versions; this entry records the limitation so it is visible, not a new request to stop. entries.evidence: The applied output format (critic finding f-s3-agent-r1-4) tells the agent to return 'tokens_used: null  # not measurable from inside this agent; never estimate it'. The dispatch schema, .ctoc/architecture/dispatch-schema.yaml line 134, types that field 'tokens_used: { type: integer, minimum: 0 }', and line 132 makes it required. So the honest value the file now orders does not satisfy the schema's type. Nothing breaks today: the only source file that names that schema, src/lib/v8-dispatcher.js, is listed as unreachable in .ctoc/reachability-baseline.json, and every fence that reads the agent file passed after the edit. Two other agents (agents/coordinator/ivv-chief.md line 187, agents/coordinator/synthesizer.md line 215) show 'tokens_used: <int>'. The executor applied the proposal exactly, as ordered, and did not change it; which side moves is a change to a machine-read contract and belongs to the human.

options.label: Keep the agent's null and widen the schema so tokens_used may be null when an agent cannot measure it
options.pros: The agent never reports a number it did not measure (Operating Lesson 18); the same rule can then apply to every agent that cannot see its own token count.
options.cons: A change to the dispatch schema, outside this slice's files, needing its own approved change; any future reader that sums tokens must handle null.

options.label: Change the agent's instruction so it emits an integer, as the schema and two coordinator agents show
options.pros: The agent's response matches the schema as written, with no schema change.
options.cons: An agent cannot read its own token count, so any integer it writes is an estimate or a placeholder presented as a measurement; that reverses a line the critic added for honesty.

entries.evidence: The French Cybersecurity Agency and the German Federal Office for Information Security, joint report "AI Coding Assistants" (https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/KI/ANSSI_BSI_AI_Coding_Assistants.pdf, last updated September 2024), page 8, read by the executor from the saved copy: "There are further risks, such as potential licensing violations when using AI-generated code, which have no direct security connection and are not addressed in the following." No agent's description claims to detect licensed code reproduced into a change: agents/compliance/license-scanner.md line 3 describes it as scanning dependencies for license compliance. The report gives no detection method. The agent critic (dispatch d-s3-agent-r3-critic, finding f-s3-agent-r3-9) proposed no text change: routing it to license-scanner would be a hand-on that agent's description does not claim, and adding a class to this agent would need a method no source gives. Filling the gap would change a file outside this slice (license-scanner or a new agent), so it is put to the human as a scheduling decision.

options.cons: A further change to this agent file in a later round or slice; with no method, what counts as suspected stays a reviewer's judgement.

entries.evidence: Google's engineering practices guide, what to look for in a code review (https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html, read 2026-09-30, by the citation validator under dispatch d-s3-skill-r2-research): "In general, tests should be added in the same CL as the production code unless the CL is handling an emergency." The reviewer checks tests that exist (vacuous tests, tests changed to pass) but not a change that adds production code with no tests at all; neither the agent's ten classes nor its hand-on list carries that case. entries.evidence: The agent needs Bash to query a registry and read the status code, so a package name taken from untrusted code can reach a shell. Round 1 added a character check the agent performs itself, single quotes, and a second check inside each recipe; all three are instructions, nothing enforces them, and the second check cannot catch a single quote. tests/watcher-shape.test.js lines 94-100 call Bash "a write tool wearing a read tool's coat". The only enforcement point would be the Bash pre-tool hook, src/hooks/PreToolUse.Bash.js, which is outside this slice. This is a decision on how much risk to accept. The Step 13 security review (dispatch d-s4-step13-secure, Info 3) adds the general point: the agent's read-only use of Bash is itself an instruction, not a fence; the grant is unrestricted, and a command the shell-write coverage check cannot identify as a write is not stopped by it.

options.cons: A change to a security hook, which needs its own approved plan; the hook must be able to tell which agent is running, which was not checked.

entries.evidence: Round 2 added a rule for a private-looking name that the public registry answers with status 200: the agent records it as a possible dependency confusion, with "no owning agent named here", and never treats REGISTERED as settling it (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts threat model, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.1/threats: "Register a package name in a public registry that shadows a name used on the victim's internal registry"). Settling it would mean querying the organisation's own private registry, which needs a recipe, credentials and a scope this agent was never given. Whether to give it those is a decision about risk and scope.

entries.evidence: Round 3 made the npm recipe print whether the latest version carries provenance (provenance=present) or was published through trusted publishing (trusted_publisher=yes), read from https://registry.npmjs.org/<name>. The agent can report that provenance is present; it cannot report that it is valid, because verifying a signature needs a tool its grant (Read, Grep, Bash) does not hold, and the file forbids reporting provenance as verified. The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity's draft advisory on artificial-intelligence-assisted software development (version 0.4, table 5) says "Where available, verify package signing, integrity or provenance metadata." Whether to add verification, and at what cost, is a decision about risk.

options.label: Keep the agent reading only whether provenance is present
options.pros: No new tool or dependency; the file already says provenance is never reported as verified.
options.cons: A package with forged or mismatched provenance reads the same as one with valid provenance.

options.label: Give the agent a way to verify provenance signatures
options.pros: The agent could tell valid provenance from present provenance.
options.cons: Needs a verification tool or dependency and a change to the agent's tool grant, which the plan keeps fixed; its own approved change.

entries.evidence: Round 3 limits the LOW triage tier for a renamed library: the page for technique T1195.001 (https://www.cisa.gov/eviction-strategies-tool/info-attack/T1195.001, carrying the same words as https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/001/, both read 2026-09-30) says a supply-chain compromise "may also include abandoned packages, which in some cases could be re-registered by threat actors after being removed by adversaries". The rule triages a renamed library as LOW only when the registry answer shows the maintainers the well-known project has. Only the wrapper's npm recipe prints maintainers ("The PyPI, crates.io and Maven Central recipes print none of these", agents/ai-quality/hallucination-detector.md), so, applied strictly, no renamed library outside npm could ever be LOW. The files now keep LOW where the recipe prints no maintainers, with "maintainers not read" in the limitations; the same scoping is in the wrapper's renamed_package severity row (late correction). Which rule to keep is a decision about how much risk to accept. The Step 11 review (dispatch d-s4-step11-review, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-step11-review-d-s4-step11-review.md, item 7) adds the npm case: when an npm answer carries no maintainers, the recipe prints maintainers="not in the answer" and both files then treat the name as suspected_lookalike (high), while the same missing data on PyPI keeps LOW. The npm answer without maintainers is therefore handled the opposite way to PyPI. The renamed rule now also reads "shares at least one maintainer with" the well-known project, because the session's probe found react-query and @tanstack/react-query share one maintainer but not all (.ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-agent-round3-session-runs.md).

options.label: Keep the rule as written: LOW where the registry's recipe prints no maintainers (PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central); an npm answer without maintainers counts as a mismatch, so suspected_lookalike (high)
options.pros: npm, whose recipe can read maintainers, gets the stricter reading when they are missing.
options.cons: Missing maintainers mean high on npm and low elsewhere.

options.label: Keep LOW wherever maintainers were not read, npm answers without maintainers included, with "maintainers not read" in the limitations
options.pros: One rule for missing data on every registry.
options.cons: A re-registered name on npm whose answer omits maintainers is triaged LOW.

options.label: Triage a renamed library as LOW only when maintainers were read and at least one is shared; otherwise suspected_lookalike, on every registry
options.pros: A re-registered abandoned name is never triaged LOW without evidence of a shared owner.
options.cons: Every renamed library outside npm becomes suspected_lookalike, severity high.

entries.evidence: The Step 13 security review (dispatch d-s4-step13-secure, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-step13-secure-d-s4-step13-secure.md, Low 5): every package name the wrapper checks is sent to public services (npm, PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central, and npm's downloads interface) before the private-name rule is applied, and the skill's gate runs `socket ci`, which uploads the manifests to a third party. A client's internal package names can therefore leave the approved data boundary. The user-agent string names only the public repository. Which way to go is a decision about data boundaries.

entries.evidence: The citation validator's re-read after the kickbacks (dispatch d-s4-post-kickback-revalidate, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-post-kickback-revalidate-d-s4-post-kickback-revalidate.md, "Leads") found two things the PyPI recipe does not read. PyPI's JSON answer carries owner roles: sklearn has "ownership":{"organization":null,"roles":[{"role":"Owner","user":"filo"},…]} (https://pypi.org/pypi/sklearn/json, read 2026-09-30), so the recipe could print owners and let the shared-maintainer rule apply to PyPI instead of writing "maintainers not read". And PyPI's index interface serves a project-status object with "active", "archived" or "quarantined" (https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2025-08-14-project-status-markers/, read 2026-09-30); a status marker is not a hold. Either would change what the recipe prints, which is a design decision.

entries.evidence: The skill's method (skills/ai-quality/llm-security-tester/SKILL.md lines 538-554 and 610) runs Garak, PyRIT, PromptFoo and a proof-of-concept request against a live model endpoint. On a throwaway PostgreSQL 18.6 cluster an unprivileged role without BYPASSRLS ran SET app.tenant_id to another tenant and the next SELECT returned that tenant's row (.ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s5-skill-round1-session-runs.md, section 4), so the policy stops a forgotten filter but not a statement injected on the connection. Framework guides are outside this run's scope, so no slice meets the file (finding f-s5-skill-r1-65a).

entries.evidence: The architecture checker decides whether a cycle is new or pre-existing. After round 2 the dependency analyzer reports one finding per strongly connected component (its node set, every import inside it and one shortest ring through each import), while madge, which the checker names, counts rings: on six files forming two components madge 8.0.0 printed "Found 4 circular dependencies!" (.ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s6-agent-round2-session-runs.md, run 2). A new ring added inside an existing component leaves the analyzer's count unchanged. Which unit the checker compares between two runs is a decision across agents, and the checker is met in slice s44. Source: .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s6-agent-round2-critic-d-s6-agent-r2-critic.md, "For the human" item 1 (finding f-s6-agent-r2-13).

entries.evidence: The agent's report is a fixed Markdown template with no structured schema and no confidence per finding. The round-3 critic states that this is the third consecutive round the absence caps the Integration dimension (the critics scored Integration 3, 6 and 6 of 10 in rounds 1, 2 and 3; round 1 named free-form Markdown with no self-assessment, rounds 2 and 3 named the missing schema) and, under its rule for an issue that recurs three rounds, escalates it as a design question about how the wrapper is structured; round 2's critic tied it to the open item h-s6-agent-r1-wrapper-duplicates-skill. Adding a schema changes the output another agent reads, which this slice may not change on its own. Source: .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s6-agent-round3-critic-d-s6-agent-r3-critic.md, "For the human" item 2 and the score tables.
